subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — BUHLE LIMITED

The information relates to the financial year ended 28 February 2023. The business sells bicycles.

Refer to Information B (ii). Calculate the value of the closing stock of bicycles using the FIFO (first-in first-out) method.

INFORMATION B (ii) — Stock of bicycles (the FIFO method is used):

Purchases for the year:
  June 2022:      2 085 units at R1 950 per unit = R4 065 750
  September 2022: 2 215 units at R2 020 per unit = R4 474 300
  January 2023:      740 units at R2 100 per unit = R1 554 000
  Total purchases: 5 040 units = R10 094 050

NOTE:
• There were 1 009 bicycles on hand on 28 February 2023.
• 40 bicycles, purchased in January 2023, were returned to the supplier due to factory faults identified.
• A number of bicycles were stolen and must be recorded as a loss.
subQuestions.memoText:
CLOSING STOCK OF BICYCLES (FIFO) — BUHLE LTD

Units on hand at year end: 1 009 bicycles.

Under FIFO the closing stock is made up of the MOST RECENTLY purchased units:

From the January 2023 purchase: 740 − 40 returned = 700 units ✓✓ at R2 100 ✓
  700 × R2 100 = R1 470 000  (3 marks)

Still needed: 1 009 − 700 = 309 units ☑ from the September 2022 purchase at R2 020 ✓
  309 × R2 020 = R624 180  (2 marks)

Value of closing stock = 1 470 000 + 624 180 = R2 094 180 ☑ (one part correct)

Answer: R2 094 180

Teaching point: FIFO assumes the FIRST goods bought are the first ones sold, so whatever is left at year end is valued at the prices of the LATEST purchases. Work backwards from the most recent purchase, and remember to strip out the 40 faulty units returned to the supplier before using the January quantity. This R2 094 180 valuation is then used in 1.2 (trading stock deficit) and 1.3 (Inventories).
subQuestions.topic: Company Financial Statements - FIFO Stock Valuation

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — BUHLE LIMITED

Complete the Statement of Comprehensive Income (Income Statement) for the year ended 28 February 2023.

NOTE: Some amounts are provided in the ANSWER BOOK. Figures are NOT required in the shaded areas (the interest income / interest expense section and the final tax figures are provided).

INFORMATION A — Extract: balances and totals from the records on 28 February 2023:
  Ordinary share capital ......................... R20 000 000
  Debtors' control .............................. R483 110
  Fixed deposit ................................. R1 500 000
  Trading stock ................................. R2 125 380
  SARS: Income tax (provisional tax payments) ... R1 049 000
  Bank (favourable) ............................. R629 000
  Creditors' control ........................... R523 890
  Sales ........................................ R21 017 200
  Commission income ............................ R277 000
  Fee income ................................... R303 000
  Directors' fees .............................. R1 610 000
  Dividends on ordinary shares ................. R990 000

INFORMATION B — Adjustments and additional information:
(i) The business uses a mark-up of 120% on the cost of bicycles. Trade discounts totalling R336 000 have been granted and recorded (i.e. already deducted from the recorded Sales of R21 017 200).
(ii) Closing stock of bicycles (FIFO) = R2 094 180 (see 1.1). Trading stock per the books is R2 125 380; a number of bicycles were stolen and must be recorded as a loss.
(iii) Commission income, R41 000, is owed to the business.
(iv) Fee income includes R47 150 for February and March 2023. Fee income increased by 5% on 1 March 2023.
(v) Buhle Ltd rents space from Prime Storage at R330 per square metre per month. It rented 150 m² from 1 May 2022 and increased the space by 25 m² (to 175 m²) on 1 November 2022. Rent was paid until 30 April 2023.
(vi) Provide for the directors' fees owed. The two directors, Brenda and Johan, have been employed since 2020. Brenda earns R10 000 per month more than Johan, but she has not been paid for February 2023 yet. Johan took unpaid leave for the last three months of the financial year.

Provided in the ANSWER BOOK: Other income also includes bad debts recovered and sundry income; Salaries and wages, Depreciation and Sundry expenses; and the shaded section — Net profit before tax R3 737 250, Income tax R1 152 000, Net profit after tax R2 585 250.
subQuestions.memoText:
STATEMENT OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME — BUHLE LTD (year ended 28 February 2023)

Sales = R21 017 200 (given)

Cost of sales = (R9 706 000) ☑ (one part correct)
Working: (21 017 200 + 336 000) × 100/220 = 21 353 200 ÷ 2,2 = R9 706 000
Logic: recorded Sales are already net of the R336 000 trade discount, so add it back to get the full invoice value of goods sold, then divide by 2,2 (a 120% mark-up means selling price = cost × 2,2).

Gross profit = 21 017 200 − 9 706 000 = R11 311 200 ✓ (operation)

Other income:
  Commission income = 277 000 + 41 000 (accrued) = R318 000 ✓✓
  Fee income = 303 000 − 24 150 = R278 850 ☑ (one part correct)
    Working for the R24 150: the R47 150 covers February 2023 (old rate) + March 2023 (new rate, 5% higher). Let February = x, then x + 1,05x = 47 150 → x = R23 000, so March = R24 150. March falls in the NEXT financial year, so it is income received in advance and must be removed. (Equivalently 47 150 × 105/205 = R24 150.)
  Bad debts recovered + Sundry income: provided in the ANSWER BOOK.
  (Total Other income = R942 900.)

Gross operating income = 11 311 200 + 942 900 = R12 254 100 ✓ (operation)

Operating expenses = (R8 103 800) ✓ (operation: 12 254 100 − 4 150 300; accept without brackets)
  Salaries and wages / Depreciation / Sundry expenses: provided in the ANSWER BOOK.
  Trading stock deficit = 2 125 380 − 2 094 180 = R31 200 ☑☑ (loss due to theft / stock loss; do NOT give 2 125 380 or 2 094 180 as the final answer)
  Rent expense = 643 500 − 115 500 = R528 000 ☑ (one part correct)
    Working: rent runs from 1 May 2022. May–Oct 2022 (6 months) at 150 m²: 150 × 330 × 6 = R297 000. Nov 2022–Feb 2023 (4 months) at 175 m²: 175 × 330 × 4 = R231 000. Rent expense = 297 000 + 231 000 = R528 000.
    Alternatively: total amount paid (May 2022–Apr 2023) = 1 950 m²-months × R330 = R643 500; less 2 months prepaid (Mar + Apr 2023 at 175 m² = 350 m²-months × R330 = R115 500) → 643 500 − 115 500 = R528 000. The R115 500 is a prepaid expense (see 1.3).
  Directors' fees = 1 610 000 + 85 000 = R1 695 000 ☑ (one part correct)
    Working: Johan's fee is R75 000 per month and Brenda's is R75 000 + R10 000 = R85 000 per month (this reconciles the recorded R1 610 000: Johan Mar–Nov = 9 months × 75 000 = R675 000; Brenda Mar 2022–Jan 2023 = 11 months × 85 000 = R935 000). The only adjustment is to accrue Brenda's unpaid February 2023 fee of R85 000. Johan's last three months were unpaid leave, so nothing is accrued for him. The R85 000 owing is carried to Trade and other payables (see 1.3).

Operating profit = 12 254 100 − 8 103 800 = R4 150 300 ✓ (operation)

Interest income / Profit before interest expense / Interest expense: provided in the ANSWER BOOK (shaded — not required).

Net profit before tax = R3 737 250 (provided)
Income tax = (R1 152 000) (provided; this figure is transferred to SARS: Income tax in 1.3)
Net profit after tax = R2 585 250 (provided)

PENALTIES: −1 for foreign items (max −2); −1 for presentation.

Teaching points:
• A mark-up of 120% on cost means selling price = cost × 2,20. To recover cost of sales from a sales figure, work with the FULL invoice value — so trade discounts that were netted off sales must be added back first.
• Income received for a period that falls in the NEXT financial year (here, the March 2023 portion of fee income) is 'income received in advance' — a current liability — and must be taken out of this year's income.
• 'Provide for fees owed' means accrue only what has been EARNED but not yet paid (Brenda's February fee); do not accrue for a director who was on unpaid leave.

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — BUHLE LIMITED

Complete the Statement of Financial Position as at 28 February 2023.

NOTE: Some amounts are provided in the ANSWER BOOK. Figures are NOT required in the shaded areas (Fixed assets, Total assets and Total equity and liabilities are provided).

INFORMATION A (relevant balances on 28 February 2023):
  Ordinary share capital ....................... R20 000 000
  Debtors' control ............................. R483 110
  Fixed deposit ............................... R1 500 000
  Trading stock ............................... R2 125 380 (closing stock per FIFO = R2 094 180, see 1.1)
  SARS: Income tax (provisional tax payments) . R1 049 000
  Bank (favourable) .......................... R629 000
  Creditors' control ........................ R523 890

CARRIED FORWARD FROM 1.2:
  Commission income accrued (owed to the business): R41 000
  Fee income received in advance (March 2023 portion): R24 150
  Rent expense prepaid (March + April 2023): R115 500
  Directors' fees owed (Brenda's February fee): R85 000
  Income tax for the year: R1 152 000

INFORMATION B — further adjustments:
(vii) Transfer a debtor's debit balance of R2 700 from the Debtors' Ledger to his account in the Creditors' Ledger.
(viii) The company has invested in three fixed deposits of equal value (R1 500 000 in total). One of them matures on 31 May 2023.
(ix) An amount for tax is still owed to SARS on 28 February 2023.
(x) Dividends: interim dividends paid R990 000; final dividends due R2 640 000.
(xi) The debt-equity ratio on 28 February 2023 is 0,2 : 1.

NOTE: The current portion of the loan is R420 000.
subQuestions.memoText:
STATEMENT OF FINANCIAL POSITION — BUHLE LTD (as at 28 February 2023)

ASSETS

NON-CURRENT ASSETS
  Fixed assets (carrying value): provided in the ANSWER BOOK.
  Financial asset: Fixed deposit = R1 000 000 ✓✓
    Working: R1 500 000 ÷ 3 = R500 000 per deposit. The one maturing 31 May 2023 falls within 12 months, so it moves to current assets; the remaining two (R1 000 000) stay here. (Award ONE mark only if R1 500 000 is left as the final answer.)

CURRENT ASSETS = R3 860 090 (operation)
  Inventories = R2 094 180 ☑ (closing stock of bicycles, see 1.1)
  Trade and other receivables = 483 110 + 41 000 − 2 700 + 115 500 = R636 910 ☑ (one part correct)
    = Debtors' control 483 110 ✓ + accrued commission income 41 000 ✓ − debtor transferred to the Creditors' Ledger 2 700 ✓ + prepaid rent expense 115 500 ✓ (one mark)
  Cash and cash equivalents = 629 000 + 500 000 = R1 129 000 ☑ (one part correct)
    = Bank (favourable) 629 000 ✓ + fixed deposit maturing 31 May 2023 500 000 ✓ (matures within 3 months of year end, so it is a cash equivalent)

TOTAL ASSETS: provided / shaded.

EQUITY AND LIABILITIES

ORDINARY SHAREHOLDERS' EQUITY = R22 562 750 ✓✓
  Working: the debt-equity ratio is non-current liabilities : shareholders' equity = 0,2 : 1, and non-current liabilities (Loan) = R4 512 550, so shareholders' equity = 4 512 550 ÷ 0,2 = R22 562 750.
  Ordinary share capital = R20 000 000 (given)
  Retained income = 22 562 750 − 20 000 000 = R2 562 750 ☑ (shareholders' equity − ordinary share capital; do NOT accept 0 as the answer)

NON-CURRENT LIABILITIES = R4 512 550
  Loan = R4 512 550 (the total Loan: Uhlula Bank less the R420 000 current portion)

CURRENT LIABILITIES = R3 793 340 (operation) ☑
  Trade and other payables = 523 890 + 24 150 + 85 000 − 2 700 = R630 340 ☑ (one part correct)
    = Creditors' control 523 890 ✓ + fee income received in advance 24 150 ☑ + directors' fees owed 85 000 ☑ − debtor transferred from the Debtors' Ledger 2 700 ✓
  Current portion of loan = R420 000
  SARS: Income tax = 1 152 000 − 1 049 000 = R103 000 ☑ (one part correct)
    = Income tax for the year 1 152 000 ✓ − provisional tax payments already made 1 049 000 ✓ = the amount still owed to SARS (a current liability; the provisional payments MUST be subtracted)
  Shareholders for dividends = R2 640 000 ✓ (final dividends due, Information B(x))

TOTAL EQUITY AND LIABILITIES: provided / shaded.

TOTAL MARKS: 55 (Question 1)

PENALTIES: −1 foreign item (max −2); −1 presentation.

Teaching points:
• The debt-equity ratio links non-current debt to equity. Given one side and the ratio, you can solve for the other: shareholders' equity = non-current liabilities ÷ 0,2.
• A fixed deposit is a non-current (financial) asset only for the portion maturing MORE than 12 months away; a portion maturing within about 3 months of year end is a cash equivalent, and anything in between is a current asset.
• A 'transfer from the Debtors' Ledger to the Creditors' Ledger' means one person is both a debtor and a creditor — his R2 700 debit is set off, which REDUCES trade and other payables and also reduces trade and other receivables.

questions.title: Cash Flow Statement and Financial Indicators (Sherbiz Ltd)

subQuestions.questionText:
CASH FLOW STATEMENT AND FINANCIAL INDICATORS — SHERBIZ LTD

The information relates to Sherbiz Ltd for the financial year ended 28 February 2023.

Prepare the Ordinary Share Capital Note for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION A — Share capital and dividends:
  1 March 2022:     1 200 000 shares in issue
  30 June 2022:     an additional 300 000 shares were issued
  1 December 2022:  90 000 shares were repurchased from a retired shareholder. He was paid R0,80 above the average share price and would no longer qualify for dividends.

INFORMATION B — from the Statement of Financial Position on 28 February:
                              2023 (R)      2022 (R)
  Ordinary share capital .... 9 306 000     7 200 000
subQuestions.memoText:
ORDINARY SHARE CAPITAL NOTE — SHERBIZ LTD (28 February 2023)

                                                       No. of shares          R
Shares in issue on 1 March 2022 ...............         1 200 000        7 200 000  (given)
Shares issued on 30 June 2022 ................           300 000 ✓      2 700 000 ☑  (balancing figure)
Shares repurchased on 1 Dec 2022 (at ASP R6,60) .       (90 000) ✓       (594 000) ☑
Shares in issue on 28 February 2023 ..........         1 410 000 ☑      9 306 000 ✓  (given)

Workings:
• Number of shares at year end = 1 200 000 + 300 000 − 90 000 = 1 410 000 (one part correct; must include the 1 200 000).
• Average share price (ASP) = R9 306 000 ÷ 1 410 000 = R6,60 per share.
• Shares repurchased are removed at the AVERAGE price: 90 000 × R6,60 = R594 000. (Do NOT use 90 000 × R0,80.)
• The R2 700 000 value of the 30 June issue is the balancing figure: 9 306 000 + 594 000 − 7 200 000 = R2 700 000 (i.e. the new shares were issued at R9,00 each).

−1 for poor presentation (max −1).

Teaching point: When shares are repurchased, only the AVERAGE-price portion (90 000 × R6,60 = R594 000) comes out of ordinary share capital in this note. The R0,80 per share paid ABOVE the average price (the 'premium', 90 000 × R0,80 = R72 000) is charged against retained income instead — it never appears in the Ordinary Share Capital Note.

subQuestions.label: 2.2 (Cash flow from operating activities)
subQuestions.questionText:
CASH FLOW STATEMENT AND FINANCIAL INDICATORS — SHERBIZ LTD

Complete the CASH FLOW FROM OPERATING ACTIVITIES section of the Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 28 February 2023, showing Dividends paid and Income tax paid. (Cash generated from operations and Interest paid, R117 600, are provided in the ANSWER BOOK.)

INFORMATION A — Share capital: 1 200 000 shares in issue on 1 March 2022; 300 000 shares issued on 30 June 2022 (bringing the total to 1 500 000); 90 000 shares repurchased on 1 December 2022.

INFORMATION B — from the Statement of Financial Position on 28 February:
                              2023 (R)        2022 (R)
  SARS: Income tax ......... 27 800 (Cr)     42 500 (Dr)
  Shareholders for dividends .. 282 000            ?

INFORMATION D — Net profit and income tax:
  • Net profit after tax amounted to R912 500.
  • Income tax is calculated at 27% of the net profit (before tax).

INFORMATION E — Dividends and earnings per share:
  Final dividends per share on 28 February 2022 ......... 24,0 cents
  Interim dividends per share paid on 31 August 2022 .... 30,0 cents
  Final dividends per share on 28 February 2023 ......... ? (final dividends of R282 000 were declared)

NOTE: All shareholders in the share register at year end qualify for dividends.
subQuestions.memoText:
CASH FLOW FROM OPERATING ACTIVITIES — SHERBIZ LTD

Interest paid = (R117 600) (provided)

Dividends paid = (R738 000) ☑ (must be in brackets)
  Working: final dividend for 2022, paid in 2023 = opening Shareholders for dividends = 1 200 000 shares × 24 cents = R288 000 ✓✓
  Plus interim dividend paid on 31 August 2022 = 1 500 000 shares × 30 cents = R450 000 ✓✓
  Dividends paid = 288 000 + 450 000 = R738 000
  (The R282 000 final dividend declared for 2023 is still a liability at year end — not yet paid.)
  OR, using total dividends: opening SFD 288 000 + total dividends for the year (interim 450 000 + final declared 282 000 = 732 000) − closing SFD 282 000 = R738 000.

Income tax paid = (R267 200) ☑
  Working: income tax expense for the year = 912 500 × 27/73 = R337 500 ✓✓ (net profit after tax is 73% of net profit before tax, so net profit before tax = 912 500 ÷ 0,73 = R1 250 000; tax = 1 250 000 × 27% = R337 500).
  Tax paid = 337 500 − 42 500 (opening SARS debit balance — tax the company had prepaid) − 27 800 (closing SARS credit balance — tax still owed) = R267 200 ✓ ✓
  OR: −337 500 + 42 500 + 27 800 (using the reversed sign convention consistently).

−1 for poor presentation (max −1).

Teaching points:
• Dividends PAID in cash this year = the previous year's final dividend (a liability at the start of the year) plus this year's interim dividend. This year's final dividend is only DECLARED, not paid, so it stays a liability.
• The number of shares matters for each dividend: the 2022 final was on the 1 200 000 shares then in issue; the interim (31 Aug 2022) was on 1 500 000 shares (after the 30 June issue).
• An opening SARS debit balance means tax was overpaid last year; a closing SARS credit balance means tax is still owed. Both reduce the cash actually paid to SARS this year.

subQuestions.label: 2.2 (Cash flow from financing activities)
subQuestions.questionText:
CASH FLOW STATEMENT AND FINANCIAL INDICATORS — SHERBIZ LTD

Complete the CASH FLOW FROM FINANCING ACTIVITIES section of the Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION A — Share capital: 300 000 shares were issued on 30 June 2022; 90 000 shares were repurchased on 1 December 2022 at R0,80 above the average share price of R6,60 (see 2.1).

INFORMATION C — Loan Statement from Megan Bank (2023):
  • Balance on 28 February 2023: R1 678 600
  • Interest capitalised for the financial year: R117 600
  • Monthly payments (including interest): R22 750

Proceeds from the 30 June 2022 share issue = R2 700 000 (see the Ordinary Share Capital Note, 2.1).
subQuestions.memoText:
CASH FLOW FROM FINANCING ACTIVITIES — SHERBIZ LTD

Proceeds from shares issued = R2 700 000 ☑ (see 2.1; no brackets)

Funds used to repurchase shares = (R666 000) ✓ ☑
  Working: 90 000 × R6,60 (average share price, see 2.1) = R594 000, plus 90 000 × R0,80 (premium paid above the ASP) = R72 000. Total cash paid = 594 000 + 72 000 = R666 000.

Change in loan = (R155 400) ✓ ☑
  Working: total instalments paid during the year = R22 750 × 12 = R273 000. Of this, R117 600 was interest (capitalised into the loan), so the capital repaid = 273 000 − 117 600 = R155 400.
  OR: opening loan balance = R1 834 000 (closing R1 678 600 + R155 400 capital repaid); change = 1 834 000 − 1 678 600 = R155 400 outflow.

Net cash from financing activities = 2 700 000 − 666 000 − 155 400 = R1 878 600 ☑ (one part correct)

Teaching point: The FULL cash paid to repurchase shares (average-price portion R594 000 + premium R72 000 = R666 000) is the financing-activities outflow — unlike the Ordinary Share Capital Note, which shows only the R594 000 average-price portion. On the loan, only the CAPITAL portion of the instalments (R155 400) is a financing outflow; the interest portion (R117 600) is shown separately under operating activities.
subQuestions.topic: Cash Flow Statement - Financing Activities

subQuestions.label: 2.3 (Net asset value per share)
subQuestions.questionText:
CASH FLOW STATEMENT AND FINANCIAL INDICATORS — SHERBIZ LTD

Calculate the net asset value per share (NAV) on 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION B — from the Statement of Financial Position on 28 February 2023:
  Ordinary shareholders' equity .... R10 200 000

Shares in issue on 28 February 2023 = 1 410 000 (see 2.1).
subQuestions.memoText:
NET ASSET VALUE PER SHARE — SHERBIZ LTD

Working: 10 200 000 ✓ ÷ 1 410 000 ☑ (see 2.1) × 100/1
= 723,4 cents ☑ (one part correct)

Answer: 723,4 cents (accept R7,23 or 723c; assume cents if not specified)

Teaching point: NAV per share is the ordinary shareholders' equity (the net worth of the company belonging to ordinary shareholders) divided by the number of shares actually in issue at year end — it is the book value backing each share, useful to compare against the market price.

subQuestions.label: 2.3 (Dividend pay-out rate)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the dividend pay-out rate for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION D — Net profit after tax: R912 500.
INFORMATION E — Interim dividends per share paid 31 August 2022: 30,0 cents. Earnings per share on 28 February 2023: 66,2 cents. Final dividends of R282 000 were declared for the year ended 28 February 2023.
Shares in issue on 28 February 2023 = 1 410 000 (see 2.1). Interim dividend paid = R450 000 (1 500 000 shares × 30 cents).
subQuestions.memoText:
DIVIDEND PAY-OUT RATE — SHERBIZ LTD

Choose ONE option and mark it consistently.

OPTION 1 (per share):
  Final dividend per share for 2023 = 282 000 ÷ 1 410 000 = 20 cents ✓✓
  Dividends per share for the year = 20 (final) + 30 (interim, given) ✓ = 50 cents
  Pay-out rate = 50 ÷ 66,2 (EPS) ✓ × 100 = 75,5% ☑ (one part correct; must be a %; accept 75% / 76% / 80%)
  (Accept (0,2 + 0,3) ÷ 0,662 × 100.)

OPTION 2 (rand totals):
  Total dividends for the year = interim 450 000 + final declared 282 000 = R732 000
  Pay-out rate = 732 000 ÷ 912 500 × 100 = 80,2%
  (450 000 = one mark; 282 000 = two marks; 732 000 = three marks; 912 500 denominator = one mark.)

Answer: 75,5% (Option 1) OR 80,2% (Option 2) — both accepted.

Teaching point: The dividend pay-out rate is the portion of earnings handed to shareholders as dividends. Option 1 (per share) and Option 2 (rand totals) give slightly different answers only because of per-share rounding — either method is acceptable as long as it is applied consistently.
subQuestions.topic: Financial Indicators - Dividend Pay-out Rate

subQuestions.label: 2.3 (% return on average shareholders' equity)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the % return on average shareholders' equity for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION D — Net profit after tax: R912 500.
INFORMATION B — Ordinary shareholders' equity: 28 February 2023 R10 200 000; 28 February 2022 R7 985 500.
subQuestions.memoText:
% RETURN ON AVERAGE SHAREHOLDERS' EQUITY — SHERBIZ LTD

Working: 912 500 ✓ ÷ [½ × (10 200 000 + 7 985 500)] × 100/1
= 912 500 ÷ ½(18 185 500) ✓✓
= 912 500 ÷ 9 092 750 × 100 ✓ (method mark on the answer)
= 10,0% ☑ (one part correct; % sign not necessary)

Answer: 10,0%

Notes from the marking guideline: the '× 100' is not 'one part correct'; numerators and denominators must be marked as such; do not award marks for operations done on a stand-alone R912 500 (no mark if anything is added to it).

Teaching point: Returns are measured against the AVERAGE equity for the year (opening + closing, ÷ 2) because the equity base changed over the period (new shares issued, shares repurchased, profits retained). Comparing the 10,0% return against the interest a fixed deposit would earn tells shareholders whether their risk is being rewarded.

questions.title: Interpretation of Financial Information (Guardian Ltd and Navarra Ltd)

subQuestions.questionText:
INTERPRETATION OF FINANCIAL INFORMATION — GUARDIAN LTD AND NAVARRA LTD

The information relates to TWO companies.

Choose an explanation from COLUMN B that matches the individual or term in COLUMN A. Write only the letter (A–D) next to the question numbers (3.1.1 to 3.1.3).

COLUMN A:
  3.1.1  Director
  3.1.2  Unqualified audit report
  3.1.3  Shareholder

COLUMN B:
  A  no opinion was expressed on the financial position of the company
  B  the person who invests funds in a company
  C  manages the operating, financing and investing activities of a company
  D  the financial statements fairly present the financial position of the company
subQuestions.memoText:
3.1.1  C ✓  (a director manages the operating, financing and investing activities of a company)
3.1.2  D ✓  (an unqualified audit report states that the financial statements fairly present the financial position of the company)
3.1.3  B ✓  (a shareholder is the person who invests funds in a company)

(Option A — 'no opinion was expressed' — describes a disclaimer of opinion, not an unqualified report.)

Teaching point: An unqualified (clean) report is the BEST audit outcome — 'fairly presents'. A disclaimer, where the auditor expresses NO opinion (usually because they could not obtain enough evidence), is the worst.

subQuestions.questionText:
Liquidity:

Identify the company that is managing its working capital well. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures and trends.

INFORMATION D — Financial indicators:
                                     GUARDIAN LTD              NAVARRA LTD
                                  28 Feb 2023  28 Feb 2022  28 Feb 2023  28 Feb 2022
  Current ratio ..............     1,7 : 1      1,5 : 1      0,9 : 1      2,5 : 1
  Acid-test ratio ...........      1,2 : 1      1,0 : 1      0,2 : 1      1,4 : 1
  Debtors' collection period      19 days      22 days      45 days      40 days
  Creditors' payment period       50 days      48 days      55 days      60 days
subQuestions.memoText:
Company: GUARDIAN LTD ✓
(If the wrong company is identified, award marks for the correct financial indicators only, max 2. Explanation beyond figures and trends is not required; trends may be implied.)

Any TWO financial indicators with figures and trends ✓✓ ✓✓ (indicator + figures/trend):
• Current ratio increased (from 1,5 : 1) to 1,7 : 1 / by 0,2 : 1.
• Acid-test ratio increased (from 1,0 : 1) to 1,2 : 1 / by 0,2 : 1.
• Debtors' collection period decreased / improved (from 22 days) to 19 days / by 3 days.
• Creditors' payment period increased (from 48 days) to 50 days / by 2 days (taking a little longer to pay creditors, which eases cash flow).

(Candidates may also motivate by pointing to the negatives at Navarra Ltd: current ratio down from 2,5 : 1 to 0,9 : 1; acid-test down from 1,4 : 1 to 0,2 : 1.)

Teaching point: 'Managing working capital well' means collecting from debtors faster, paying creditors no faster than necessary, and keeping the liquidity ratios healthy. Guardian improved on every measure; Navarra deteriorated sharply.

subQuestions.label: 3.3 (Causes of the change in the debt-equity ratio)
subQuestions.questionText:
Financing strategies and gearing: GUARDIAN LTD

What were the causes of the change in the debt-equity ratio? Provide TWO causes with figures.

INFORMATION B — extracts for Guardian Ltd:
                              28 Feb 2023 (R)   28 Feb 2022 (R)
  Ordinary share capital ....  20 960 000        12 000 000
  Mortgage loan ...........     5 000 000         3 600 000
  (An additional 800 000 shares were issued at R11,20 during the year.)

INFORMATION D — Guardian Ltd debt-equity ratio: 0,2 : 1 (2023); 0,3 : 1 (2022).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO causes with figures ✓✓ ✓✓:
• Increase in the loan from R3 600 000 to R5 000 000 / by R1 400 000 / by 38,8%.
• Increase in ordinary share capital (OSC) from R12 000 000 to R20 960 000 / by R8 960 000 / by 74,6% / by issuing an additional 800 000 shares.

Teaching point: The debt-equity ratio still IMPROVED (0,3 : 1 down to 0,2 : 1) even though the loan grew in rand terms, because equity grew much faster (through the R8,96 million share issue). Gearing must be judged by the RATIO, not by the rand movement in debt alone.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Financing Strategies and Gearing

subQuestions.label: 3.3 (Why more use of loans was wise)
subQuestions.questionText:
Explain why it was wise for Guardian Ltd to make more use of loans. Quote and explain ONE other financial indicator (with figures and trends) to support this opinion. (Do NOT use the debt-equity ratio here.)

INFORMATION D — Guardian Ltd:
                                        28 Feb 2023   28 Feb 2022
  % return on average capital employed .. 16,6%         13,5%
  Interest rate on loan ...............   14%           13%
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator with figures ✓ ✓:
• % return on average capital employed (ROTCE) increased (from 13,5%) to 16,6% / by 3,1 percentage points / by 23%.

Comment must cover POSITIVE gearing relative to the interest rate ✓✓ (part-marks for an unclear or partial answer):
• The company is positively geared: the return (16,6%) is greater than the interest rate on borrowing (14%).
• The loan (which increased) was used productively — borrowed at 14% to generate a 16,6% return.
• The company was already positively geared last year (13,5% vs 13%); positive gearing improved despite the interest rate rising to 14%.

Teaching point: Borrowing is 'wise' when the money borrowed earns MORE than it costs — i.e. ROTCE > the interest rate on the loan. That gap (16,6% vs 14%) is 'positive gearing', and it means the loan is boosting the return to ordinary shareholders rather than dragging it down.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Positive Gearing

subQuestions.label: 3.4 (Change in dividend policy)
subQuestions.questionText:
Dividends, earnings and returns: NAVARRA LTD

Explain ONE financial indicator which shows that a concerned shareholder should NOT be satisfied with the change in the dividend policy of the company. Quote figures and trends.

INFORMATION D — Navarra Ltd:
                          28 Feb 2023   28 Feb 2022
  Dividend pay-out rate .. 103,8%        34,8%
  Earnings per share ....  80 cents      115 cents
  Dividends per share ...  83 cents      40 cents
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator with figures and trend ✓ ✓:
• Dividend pay-out rate increased (from 34,8%) to 103,8% / by 69 percentage points / by 198%.
• OR: dividends per share (83c) is 43c more than last year while EPS dropped from 115c to 80c / by 35c (the answer must cover BOTH EPS and DPS together).

Comment ✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial; do NOT accept just 'shareholders are / are not satisfied' — the answer must say the company is not retaining funds for future growth):
• Funds from retained income were used to pay the current year's dividends / reserves that could fund future expansion are being depleted / the directors are not concerned about future growth or sustainability / the directors may simply be trying to keep shareholders happy or secure re-election.

Teaching point: A pay-out rate over 100% means the company paid out MORE in dividends than it earned this year — it dipped into past retained profits to do so. That is unsustainable and leaves nothing for reinvestment, which is why a forward-looking shareholder would be concerned.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Dividend Policy

subQuestions.label: 3.4 (Satisfaction with earnings and returns)
subQuestions.questionText:
Explain whether the shareholders of Navarra Ltd should be satisfied with the earnings and returns of the company. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures and trends.

INFORMATION D — Navarra Ltd:
                                            28 Feb 2023   28 Feb 2022
  Earnings per share ...................... 80 cents      115 cents
  % return on average shareholders' equity  6,4%          11%
  Interest rate on fixed deposit .........  9%            8%
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicators with figures and trends ✓✓ ✓✓:
• Earnings per share (EPS) decreased (from 115 cents) to 80 cents / by 35 cents / by 30,4%.
• % return on average shareholders' equity (ROSHE) decreased (from 11%) to 6,4% / by 4,6 percentage points / by 41,8%.

Comment ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial):
• Shareholders should NOT be satisfied. The return (6,4%) is now lower than what they could earn on a safe outside investment (9% on a fixed deposit) / the fall in profitability has driven returns down.

(Do NOT accept dividends per share, earnings yield or dividend yield as the indicators here.)

Teaching point: The key test is ROSHE versus a risk-free alternative. When ROSHE (6,4%) drops below the fixed-deposit rate (9%), shareholders are carrying share-investment risk for a WORSE return than a bank would have given them — a clear reason for dissatisfaction.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Earnings and Returns

subQuestions.label: 3.5 (Effect on % shareholding)
subQuestions.questionText:
Shareholding of Nathan Crewe in NAVARRA LTD:

Identify the effect that the repurchase of Nathan's shares had on his % shareholding. Quote figures and trends.

INFORMATION C — Nathan convinced the other directors of Navarra Ltd to repurchase 300 000 of his shares for R3 450 000 on 1 September 2022. His holding fell from 662 000 shares to 362 000 shares. His % shareholding: 55,2% (2022); 40,2% (2023).
subQuestions.memoText:
Figures with trend ✓✓:
• Nathan's % shareholding dropped (from 55,2%) to 40,2% / by 15 percentage points / by 27,2%.
• ONE MARK: he is no longer the majority shareholder / his shareholding is now 40,2% (below 50%).

Teaching point: Selling shares BACK to the company (a repurchase from one shareholder only) reduces that shareholder's holding while leaving everyone else's number of shares unchanged — so his PERCENTAGE falls, and here it takes him below the 50% majority mark.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Effect of Share Repurchase on Shareholding

subQuestions.label: 3.5 (How the ~R4,4 million was raised)
subQuestions.questionText:
Explain how the company was able to raise approximately R4,4 million to finance the repurchase of Nathan's shares (R3 450 000) and the dividends earned by shareholders. Provide TWO points with figures.

INFORMATION B — Navarra Ltd:
                          28 Feb 2023 (R)   28 Feb 2022 (R)
  Mortgage loan .........  6 500 000         3 000 000
  Bank (favourable) .....       —              380 000
  Bank (overdraft) ......  3 200 000            —
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO points with figures ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ (trend may be implied):
• The loan increased by R3 500 000 (from R3 000 000 to R6 500 000).
• The bank balance moved into an overdraft of R3 200 000 — from a favourable balance of R380 000 to an overdraft of R3 200 000, a swing of R3 580 000.

Teaching point: A company with insufficient cash reserves can only fund a large repurchase by taking on more debt (the R3,5m extra loan) and/or running its bank balance down into overdraft (the R3,58m swing). Both routes here increased Navarra's financial risk considerably.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Financing a Share Repurchase

subQuestions.label: 3.5 (Why the repurchase was irresponsible)
subQuestions.questionText:
Give TWO reasons why the decision to repurchase Nathan's shares should be considered as irresponsible.

INFORMATION — the shares were repurchased at R11,50 per share (1 150 cents). Navarra Ltd's market price per share fell from 1 800 cents (2022) to 400 cents (2023). The repurchase created a bank overdraft of R3 200 000, and the current ratio fell to 0,9 : 1 and the acid-test ratio to 0,2 : 1. (Do NOT use 'loss of majority shareholding' as a reason here.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO different reasons (e.g. one on ethics, one on affordability) ✓✓ ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial):
• The repurchase price of 1 150 cents was high while the market price was falling over the year (to 400 cents).
• It does not comply with the law on the funding of repurchased shares / it contravenes the Companies Act.
• The company did not comply with the solvency and liquidity test / it compromised liquidity / it created a large overdraft and cash-flow problem / it placed the company in a risky financial position.
• Company profitability had declined — the buy-back was unaffordable.
• Nathan misused his majority status to benefit from the repurchase / he promoted his own selfish interest at the expense of the company / there is an element of corruption (he may have used privileged information).
• The decision contributed to the decline in several key financial indicators.

Teaching point: A director persuading the board to buy HIS shares — at an inflated price, funded by overdraft, when the company cannot afford it — breaches both the Companies Act's solvency-and-liquidity requirement and basic ethics (conflict of interest / self-enrichment).
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Irresponsible Share Repurchase

subQuestions.label: 3.6 (Influence of the CFO)
subQuestions.questionText:
Directorship:

'The CFO (chief financial officer) has a significant influence on the success of a company.' Explain why you would agree with this statement. Provide ONE point.

BACKGROUND: Sheryl Mabaso is the CFO of Guardian Ltd (which performed well) and Nathan Crewe is the CFO of Navarra Ltd (which performed poorly). Sheryl will retire in March 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
ONE point ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial):
• The CFO must be an expert in accounting and financial management, tasked with safeguarding the stakeholders' investment.
• As head of finance, the CFO is responsible for sound financial management, advising the board, leading by example and displaying good corporate governance (ethics and professionalism).
• The CFO should be aware of the company's performance, financial position and available resources, and should create the structure for sound checks and balances (internal controls).
• The CFO should not place the business at risk, should focus on growth and sustainability, and should report regularly and transparently.

Teaching point: The contrast in the question makes the point — the same role, two CFOs, opposite outcomes. The CFO sets the tone for financial discipline, risk management and reporting integrity, all of which feed directly into whether the company succeeds.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Role of the CFO

subQuestions.label: 3.6 (Satisfaction with the share prices)
subQuestions.questionText:
Explain whether the directors should be satisfied or not with the share prices of the companies at the end of the financial year. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures in EACH case.

INFORMATION D:
                              GUARDIAN LTD              NAVARRA LTD
  Net asset value per share .. 1 230 cents              992 cents
  Market price per share ....  1 350 cents              400 cents
  (Guardian's market price rose from 1 150c; Navarra's fell from 1 800c.)
subQuestions.memoText:
GUARDIAN LTD — financial indicators with figures ✓ (trends not compulsory):
• NAV is 1 230 cents; market price is 1 350 cents (OR the market price increased to 1 350c while NAV is 1 230c).
Comment ✓ (must cover demand for the shares / investor confidence / the company's success — do NOT accept just 'satisfied'):
• The directors should be satisfied: the shares are in demand / investors are willing to buy / the company has a good image and has performed well (upward trend), which has pushed the market price above NAV.

NAVARRA LTD — financial indicators with figures ✓ (trends not compulsory):
• NAV is 992 cents; market price is 400 cents (OR the market price dropped to 400c while NAV dropped to 992c).
Comment ✓ (must cover lack of demand / investor pessimism / lack of success — do NOT accept just 'not satisfied'):
• The directors should NOT be satisfied: the shares are not in demand due to a poor image / few potential investors / the drastic drop in market price signals serious management problems.

Teaching point: When the market price sits ABOVE net asset value (Guardian: 1 350c vs 1 230c), the market is optimistic about the company's future. When it falls far BELOW NAV (Navarra: 400c vs 992c), investors have lost confidence and are valuing the shares at less than their book worth.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation - Share Prices and Net Asset Value

subQuestions.label: 3.6 (Advice to the CEO)
subQuestions.questionText:
The CEO (chief executive officer) of Guardian Ltd intends to offer the vacant position of CFO to Nathan Crewe in March 2023 (when Sheryl Mabaso retires). Explain ONE point of advice to the CEO.

(Do NOT use 'qualifications' as your answer.)
subQuestions.memoText:
ONE valid point ✓✓ (part-mark for unclear / partial; do NOT accept 'qualifications'):
• Nathan takes selfish decisions at the expense of the company.
• He has no good track record — he placed Navarra at financial risk (high debt-equity, excessive borrowing, funds not used productively).
• There is limited demand for the shares of the company he managed.
• Guardian is a profitable company that must be protected — Nathan may destroy that progress.
• He does not appear to be loyal, and there is a conflict of interest as he is still involved with Navarra Ltd.
• Nepotism / appointing him despite his record is not acceptable as it can lead to corruption.
• Rather retain a reliable, capable employee — Nathan's management ruined Navarra Ltd.

Teaching point: Past conduct is the best predictor here. Nathan's decisions wrecked Navarra's finances and reputation, and he is conflicted (still tied to a rival). Appointing him to safeguard Guardian's finances would be reckless.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Advice on Appointing a Director

subQuestions.label: 4.1 (Duty of an internal auditor)
subQuestions.questionText:
CORPORATE GOVERNANCE — MONACO LTD

You are provided with an article relating to an internal auditor who lost her job (see below). Use the information and your knowledge of companies to answer the questions. Do NOT repeat responses across the different questions.

Auditing: Explain ONE duty of an internal auditor.

ARTICLE — MONACO LTD: A WHISTLE-BLOWER'S STORY
Eight months ago the internal auditor of Monaco Ltd, Sally Bolden, was fired from her well-paid position. She had exposed her bosses — new board chairperson Glen Turner and CFO Rachel Donovan — for irregular payments of R3 500 million to companies linked to them. Sally remains unemployed and is struggling to support her family. She and other whistle-blowers now regret taking a stand against corruption.
Sally's new internal control measures and her replacement of non-performing suppliers with competent ones had greatly benefitted the company: a R500 million loss in 2021 became a R280 million profit in 2022.
Her problems began when a new board, chaired by Turner, was appointed. Turner said Sally's employment was terminated for 'bringing the company into disrepute', and that the board would conduct an investigation to identify the other whistle-blowers.
The external auditors later found that a further R200 million had been paid to other individuals linked to Turner and Donovan through irregular procurement deals, and that the two had allegedly manipulated company policies to appoint their friends to the new board.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid explanation ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial):
• Set up, implement or advise on internal control processes in line with external auditing requirements.
• Oversee the preparation and carry out an internal audit of the financial statements before the external audit.
• Chair (or serve on) the internal audit committee.

Teaching point: The internal auditor works INSIDE the company year-round, checking that internal controls are sound and financial information is reliable BEFORE the external auditor arrives — exactly what Sally was doing when she uncovered the irregular payments.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Role of the Internal Auditor

subQuestions.label: 4.1 (Why an external audit is required)
subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE reason why the accounting records of a listed company must be audited by an external (independent) auditor. (See the Monaco Ltd article in 4.1.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid explanation ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial):
• It is a requirement of the Companies Act / it confirms compliance with accounting standards, principles and international reporting.
• It protects public investment and the interests of shareholders against possible mismanagement or fraud — an unbiased, independent opinion is expected.
• It complies with corporate governance / King Code requirements on ethical conduct and transparency.
• Shareholders can be confident that the financial results are reliable and credible.

Teaching point: An EXTERNAL auditor is independent of management, so their opinion carries weight the internal auditor's cannot — the Companies Act requires it for listed (public) companies precisely because the public's money is invested.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Purpose of the External Audit

subQuestions.questionText:
Whistle-blowers (informants):

In the first paragraph of the article, Sally and other whistle-blowers say they 'now regret taking a stand against corruption'. What would you say to Sally regarding this statement? Explain ONE point. (See the Monaco Ltd article in 4.1.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid explanation ✓✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial). The response must SUPPORT whistle-blowing:
• It is understandable that she feels victimised (she lost her job), but citizens should be grateful to whistle-blowers — if they do not come forward, crime cannot be brought under control.
• Whistle-blowers help to expose and minimise corrupt actions by managers and employees.
• She had no choice but to report it — as the appointed internal auditor she could have been accused of negligence for staying silent.
• She can take the company to court or the CCMA for unfair dismissal.
• Corrupt individuals think twice when they know people are watching / it promotes ethical conduct in the corporate world.
• The SA government has stated that whistle-blowers must be protected and allowed to remain anonymous.

Teaching point: The 'regret' is emotionally understandable, but the ethical answer is that reporting corruption was the RIGHT thing to do — and there are legal remedies (courts, CCMA) and legal protections for whistle-blowers she can still rely on.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Whistle-blowers

subQuestions.questionText:
Shareholders' opinions and concerns:

As a shareholder of Monaco Ltd, explain THREE points that would concern you about the actions of the board of directors of Monaco Ltd. In EACH case, give a suitable reason for your concern. (See the Monaco Ltd article in 4.1.)
subQuestions.memoText:
THREE valid and DIFFERENT concerns, each with a reason. Concerns ✓✓ ✓✓ ✓✓ + reasons ✓ ✓ ✓ (part-marks for unclear / partial). Concerns and reasons may be marked independently; do not accept a reason that merely re-words the concern.

Examples of acceptable CONCERN → REASON pairs:
• The board is investigating to identify the other whistle-blowers / whistle-blowers are not protected → their anonymity may not be respected, so employees will not speak out about further wrongdoing; the law is meant to keep their identity hidden.
• Collusion between directors and service providers / nepotism / conflict of interest (friends appointed to the board) → self-enrichment at the company's expense; financial losses that are not the result of performance; the competence of the appointees is questionable.
• Honesty and loyalty are not recognised (Sally was dismissed unfairly) / public investment is not being protected → growth in company profits may be compromised; shareholder interest in the shares may be negatively affected.
• Corruption went undetected for a long period / lack of transparency / honest employees look the other way → company policies can be manipulated; there is no accountability or checks and balances; corruption will continue with no consequences; staff fear victimisation.
• The integrity and credibility of management is in doubt / labour law and company policies (procurement, recruitment, bonuses) were breached → unfair dismissal may drag the company into a legal battle; the share price will fall as investors lose interest and shareholders sell their shares.

Teaching point: A strong answer pairs a SPECIFIC board action from the article (hunting whistle-blowers, appointing friends, irregular payments, unfair dismissal) with a concrete CONSEQUENCE for the shareholder (legal costs, a falling share price, ongoing losses, weak controls) — not two restatements of the same idea.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Shareholders' Concerns
